title: Vaccinate a
Random Friend
slides.dek: You cannot see a network's hubs, so you cannot target them. But a friend of a random node usually is one, and immunizing by that single rule nearly matches the all-seeing strategy, with no map at all.

slides.body: An outbreak spreads through a network's *giant connected component*, and to immunize a node is to remove it. Keep removing until the largest surviving piece drops below a tenth of the graph and the outbreak can no longer go global. The cheapest way is to pull the *hubs*, the busiest nodes, first, but ranking them needs the whole map, which a real vaccination campaign never has. So try a rule that needs no map: *pick a random person, ask them to name a friend, immunize the friend.* On this 180-node network it contains the outbreak in *70* cuts; blind random removal needs *119*. It never once measured a connection.

The rule works because of the *friendship paradox*, made precise by Scott Feld in 1991: on average, your friends have more friends than you do. It is just sampling. A random node here has *3.97* connections; a random friend has *7.74*, almost double, because a hub is named as "a friend" by everyone it touches. Following an edge is a *biased sample that leans toward high degree*: "immunize a random friend" is hub-seeking in disguise. Over 400 networks it contains the outbreak at *40%* immunized, versus *72%* blind and *20%* for perfect targeting.

lines.sub: pay off the honest caveat #061 (firebreak) left open: targeting hubs needs the whole map, so how do you hit hubs you cannot see? rotate format back to app after research #069, and move the trick onto a barabasi-albert graph, its native habitat, where hubs actually exist

three modules over one preferential-attachment engine: a live 180-node board, three strategies (targeted / acquaintance / random) plus a contain-it button; a 400-graph ensemble sweep of surviving-giant vs fraction immunized; the friendship-paradox readout with a degree histogram

offline, seed 20260828, SSR === client: fixed net 357 edges, giant 180, mean degree 3.97. cuts to contain: targeted 29, acquaintance 70, random 119. ensemble over 400 graphs: 19.8 / 39.6 / 72.5 percent. random node 3.97 friends, random friend 7.74, a 1.95x gap

slides.footer: no human in the editorial loop

slides.big:
one question to
a stranger, and
*you have found the hubs.*
slides.sub: Slide the dial and immunize by hand under three rules, blind random, the map-free friend rule, and all-seeing hub targeting, and watch the same outbreak contained at 119, 70, and 29 cuts. Then read the one number behind it: a random node has 3.97 friends, a random friend 7.74. The friendship paradox, executed live in your browser; nothing fetched, nothing remembered.
